title: Correcting for many tests
objectives: Apply the Bonferroni correction and control the false discovery rate.

screens.title: A budget of 5%
screens.prose: You will run 20 tests on signals that may all be noise. You want at most a 5% chance of any false alarm in the whole family. Each test needs its own, stricter threshold.

derive.caption: Each test at {{fixed(t, 4)}}: P(any false alarm) = {{fixed(1 - pow(1 - t, 20), 3)}}

screens.question: Slide to the largest per-test threshold that keeps the family's chance at or below 0.05.

hints.text: Start at 0.05 and slide left. Watch the caption.
The dashed line is 0.05. The point must sit on or below it.
Try the 5% split evenly over 20 tests: $0.05 / 20$.

feedback.correct: 0.0025 per test keeps the family at 0.049.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the last step before the caption goes above 0.05.

byKey.uncorrected: You left the threshold near 0.05. With 20 tests that gives the family about 64%.
byKey.over: The family's chance is still above 0.05 there. Slide further left.
byKey.strict: That keeps the family safe, but it is stricter than needed. Slide right until the next step would cross 0.05.

explain.text: At 0.0025 each, the family's chance is $1 - 0.9975^{20} = 0.049$. The next step, 0.003, gives 0.058. You split the 5% budget evenly: $0.05 / 20 = 0.0025$.

screens.title: Bonferroni
screens.prose: You divided $\alpha$ by the number of tests. That is the **Bonferroni correction**: test each of $N$ at $\alpha / N$. The exact cut-off for independent tests is the **Šidák** threshold $1 - (1 - \alpha)^{1/N}$: 0.00256 for $N = 20$.
screens.question: A screen runs 50 tests with a family-wise target of 0.05. What Bonferroni threshold does each test use?

hints.text: Divide the family's budget by the number of tests.
The family has 50 members and a budget of 0.05.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bonferroni uses $\alpha / N$.

byKey.none: That leaves every test at 0.05, with no correction at all.
byKey.times: You multiplied by 50. The threshold must shrink as tests are added.
byKey.twenty: That is the threshold for 20 tests. This screen has 50.

explain.text: $0.05 / 50 = 0.001$ per test, and the family's chance is then $1 - 0.999^{50} = 0.0488$. Šidák would allow 0.00103. Bonferroni is a touch stricter than it needs to be, so it is called conservative.

screens.title: Eight signals
screens.prose: A researcher tests 8 signals and sorts their $p$-values from smallest to largest. With $\alpha = 0.05$ and $N = 8$, Bonferroni compares every one with $0.05 / 8 = 0.00625$.
screens.question: Tap every signal that Bonferroni rejects.

hints.text: Compare each $p$-value with 0.00625.
Only the top of the table can be that small.
0.004 is below 0.00625. The next, 0.012, is not.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the rows with $p \le 0.00625$.

byKey.r1: Short interest has $p = 0.012$, above 0.00625. It passes 0.05 alone, but not Bonferroni.
byKey.r2: Carry has $p = 0.016$, above 0.00625. It would pass a lone test, not the corrected one.

explain.text: Only earnings drift, $p = 0.004$, sits below 0.00625. Short interest (0.012) and carry (0.016) would pass at 0.05 alone. Bonferroni gives them up to keep the chance of any false rejection at 5%.

screens.title: A bar for each rank
screens.prose: **Benjamini-Hochberg** (BH) gives each rank its own bar. Rank $k$ is compared with $k\alpha / N$: the sloped line on the chart. Ranks 5 to 8 sit above the top of the chart.
screens.question: Fill in the bar $k\alpha/N$ for each rank, with $\alpha = 0.05$ and $N = 8$.

hints.text: Rank 1's bar is the Bonferroni bar, $0.05 / 8$.
Each rank adds another 0.00625.
The bars run 0.00625, 0.0125, 0.01875, and so on up to 0.05.

feedback.correct: The bars climb from 0.00625 to 0.05 in equal steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the rank $k$ by $0.05 / 8 = 0.00625$.

byKey.r0c2: Rank 1's bar is $1 \times 0.05 / 8 = 0.00625$, the Bonferroni bar.
byKey.r7c2: The last rank's bar is $8 \times 0.05 / 8 = 0.05$: plain $\alpha$.

explain.text: The bars climb in steps of $0.05/8 = 0.00625$, from 0.00625 at rank 1 to 0.05 at rank 8. Rank 1 faces the Bonferroni bar and the last rank faces plain $\alpha$. That is why BH is less strict than Bonferroni.

screens.title: The largest rank under the line
screens.prose: BH finds the **largest** rank $k$ with $p_{(k)} \le k\alpha / N$, then rejects ranks 1 to $k$. The dots are the sorted $p$-values from the table.
screens.question: Tap the signals that BH rejects.

hints.text: Which dots sit on or under the sloped line?
Rank 4 is the first dot clearly above the line. Check the dots before it.

feedback.correct: BH rejects ranks 1, 2 and 3: three signals.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the last dot under the line, and reject it and every dot before it.

byKey.p4: Rank 4 has $p = 0.041$, above its bar of 0.025. So do all later ranks.
byKey.p1: Earnings drift is rejected, but so are ranks 2 and 3, which sit under their bars too.

explain.text: Ranks 1, 2 and 3 sit under the line: 0.004, 0.012 and 0.016 against 0.00625, 0.0125 and 0.01875. Rank 4 is above its bar, and so is every later rank. BH rejects 3 where Bonferroni rejected 1.

screens.title: What BH promises
screens.prose: BH controls the **false discovery rate** (FDR): the share of rejections that are false, on average. Bonferroni controls the FWER. Here BH at 5% rejected 3 signals.
screens.question: Which statement about the 3 rejected signals is right?

options.text: There is at most a 5% chance that any of the 3 is false
options.why: You read BH's 5% as a family-wise rate. That is Bonferroni's promise. BH bounds the average share of false rejections.

options.text: On average, at most 5% of BH's rejections are false
Each of the 3 has a 95% chance of being real
options.why: You turned 5% into a chance for each signal. BH bounds an average share over many studies, not any one signal.

options.text: Exactly 0.15 of the 3 signals are false
options.why: You took 5% of 3 as an exact count. The 5% is a bound on an average, not a count for this study.

hints.text: FWER is about the chance of even one false rejection. FDR is about a share.
Read the definition at the top: a share, on average. These are the 3 rejections it is a share of.
BH's 5% bounds the expected share of rejections that are false.

feedback.correct: FDR is an average share of false rejections, not the chance of any.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether 5% is a chance of any error or an average share.

byKey.fwer: You read BH's 5% as a family-wise rate. That is Bonferroni's promise, and it bought only 1 rejection here.

explain.text: BH promises that false rejections make up at most 5% of its rejections, on average over studies (for independent tests). It does not promise a 95% chance of no false ones. That stronger promise is Bonferroni's, and it kept only 1 signal here.

screens.title: A family of one
screens.prose: Edge case. A researcher runs a single test, fixed in advance, at $\alpha = 0.05$. So $N = 1$.
screens.question: Which method changes the threshold for a single test?

options.why: $\alpha / N$ with $N = 1$ is $\alpha$ itself. Nothing changes.
Rank 1 of 1 has bar $1 \times \alpha / 1 = \alpha$. Nothing changes.

hints.text: Put $N = 1$ into each rule.
With one test the only rank is $k = 1$.
$\alpha/1$, $1 - (1-\alpha)^1$ and $1 \cdot \alpha/1$ are all $\alpha$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $N = 1$ into each rule in the table.

explain.text: Put $N = 1$ into each rule: $\alpha/1$, $1 - (1-\alpha)^1$ and $1 \cdot \alpha / 1$ all equal $\alpha$. The corrections bite only when there is more than one test. A single test, fixed in advance, needs none.

screens.title: Why Bonferroni works
screens.prose: Why does $\alpha/N$ hold the FWER at $\alpha$, even when tests are dependent? Let $A_i$ be the event that true null $i$ is rejected. You met the union bound in *The rules every probability obeys*.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $\text{FWER} = P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \dots \cup A_N)$, at least one false rejection
$\le P(A_1) + P(A_2) + \dots + P(A_N)$, by the union bound
$= N \cdot \dfrac{\alpha}{N}$, since each true null is rejected with chance $\alpha / N$

hints.text: Start from what FWER means as an event.
The inequality comes from the union bound, before any numbers go in.
Event, union bound, each term $\alpha/N$, then cancel.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the FWER as a union first, then bound it.

byKey.each: Substituting $\alpha / N$ needs the sum of the $P(A_i)$ first, from the union bound.

explain.text: The union bound needs no independence, so Bonferroni holds whatever the dependence between tests. The price is slack: overlaps are counted twice, so the true FWER is usually below $\alpha$. That slack is what conservative means.

screens.title: Screening 500 stocks
screens.prose: You test 500 stocks for a momentum effect, one test each, and run BH with $q = 0.10$. The six smallest $p$-values are below. Every later rank is above its bar.
screens.question: How many stocks survive BH at 10%?

widget.label: Number of stocks BH rejects
widget.accept: 4 exactly: ranks 1 to 4 are under their bars, rank 5 is not.

hints.text: Work out each rank's bar, $0.0002k$.
Rank 5 has $p = 0.0011$ against a bar of 0.0010.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each $p_{(k)}$ with $0.0002k$, and keep up to the largest rank that passes.

byKey.bonf: That is Bonferroni at 10%: $p \le 0.0002$ for every test. BH lets later ranks face higher bars.
byKey.all: Rank 5 (0.0011) and rank 6 (0.0019) are above their bars, 0.0010 and 0.0012.
byKey.first: Rank 1 passes, but ranks 2 to 4 pass their own, higher bars too.
byKey.five: Rank 5 has $p = 0.0011$, just above its bar of 0.0010.

explain.text: The bars are 0.0002, 0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0008, 0.0010 and 0.0012. Ranks 1 to 4 sit under theirs; ranks 5 and 6 do not. With FDR held at 10%, we expect at most about 0.4 of the 4 to be false.

screens.title: BH in code
screens.prose: A screen of hundreds of signals needs BH done by code. Sort the indices by $p$-value, find the largest rank $r$ with $p_{(r)} \le rq/n$, and reject the first $r$. The function returns the rejected indices in their original order.

state.caption: The 8 signals from the table: BH rejects the first three.

screens.question: Complete `bh_reject`.

widget.starter:
def bh_reject(pvals, q=0.05):
    """Indices, in the original order, that BH rejects at level q."""
    n = len(pvals)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: pvals[i])
    k = 0
    # find the largest rank r (1 to n) with p_(r) <= r * q / n
    ...
    return sorted(order[:k])

print(bh_reject([0.004, 0.012, 0.016, 0.041, 0.10, 0.22, 0.48, 0.73]))
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, each compared for equality with the list of rejected indices. They include shuffled input, a rank that fails before a later one passes, $n = 1$, ties and a 500-stock screen at $q = 0.10$. Pure Python is enough; numpy and scipy are available but load slowly the first time.

hints.text: Loop over `enumerate(order, start=1)` to get each rank `r` and index `i`.
Do not stop at the first failure: a later rank can still pass.
Inside the loop: `if pvals[i] <= r * q / n: k = r`.

feedback.correct: BH keeps the largest passing rank, then rejects everything up to it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the largest rank that passes, even after a failure.

explain.text: The loop records the last rank under its bar, so a failure part-way does not stop it. `order[:k]` are the indices of the $k$ smallest $p$-values. Sorting them returns the original order.

ideas: Bonferroni tests each of $N$ at $\alpha/N$. The union bound keeps the family-wise error rate at or below $\alpha$, for any dependence.
Benjamini-Hochberg compares the $k$-th smallest $p$-value with $k\alpha/N$ and rejects up to the largest $k$ that passes. It controls the false discovery rate.
FWER bounds the chance of any false rejection; FDR bounds their average share. With $N = 1$ every method is plain $\alpha$.

formula.name: Benjamini-Hochberg
formula.tex: \text{reject } p_{(1)}, \dots, p_{(k)} \text{ for the largest } k \text{ with } p_{(k)} \le \dfrac{k\alpha}{N}
formula.note: Bonferroni is the flat bar $\alpha/N$ at every rank.

summary.trap: BH at 5% is not a 5% chance of any false discovery. That is the FWER, Bonferroni's promise.

quiz.prose: A desk tests 40 signals and wants a family-wise error rate of at most 0.05.
quiz.question: What Bonferroni threshold should each test use?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\alpha$ by the number of tests.

byKey.none: That is no correction at all.
byKey.times: You multiplied by 40. The threshold must shrink.

explain.text: Bonferroni splits the 0.05 budget over 40 tests: $0.05 / 40 = 0.00125$ each. The union bound then keeps the FWER at or below 0.05, whatever the dependence.

quiz.prose: A team wants to bound the average share of its discoveries that are false, and accepts a few false ones.
quiz.question: Which method fits?

options.why: Bonferroni bounds the chance of any false discovery, the FWER. It is stricter than this team needs.
Šidák also bounds the FWER, for independent tests.
With no correction, the share of false discoveries is not bounded at all.

feedback.correct: BH controls the false discovery rate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match an average share of false discoveries to its method.

explain.text: An average share of false discoveries is the false discovery rate, which BH controls. Bonferroni and Šidák control the chance of even one false discovery. That is stricter, and finds less.

quiz.prose: For 10 independent tests and a family-wise target of 0.05, the Šidák threshold is $1 - (1 - 0.05)^{1/10}$.
quiz.question: Compute it to 6 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise 0.95 to the power 0.1, then subtract from 1.

byKey.bonf: That is Bonferroni, $0.05/10$. Šidák is a little larger.
byKey.pow: You raised 0.95 to the power 10. The power is $1/10$.

explain.text: $0.95^{0.1} = 0.994884$, so the threshold is $1 - 0.994884 = 0.005116$. Bonferroni's 0.005 is just below it. The gap is why Bonferroni is called conservative.
